scope.operations: Secret and WorkArea construction, byte access and wipe/drop; ClosedSecret closure/reopening and lock state; isolation entry, all seven options, 19 protection outcomes and reach, required/process-wide checks; WritableFolder identity and privacy; channel census; character/frame encoding, line edit and native input/output; protected stack and current-thread wipe.

findings.title: Linux worker pipes are exposed through the launcher
findings.evidence: Independent source traces and the Linux procfs and ptrace ABI. Yama attach restrictions alone leave the descriptor read-mode check outside their scope. A parent-side dumpability check alone also leaves a worker initialization interval because ordinary exec restores its dumpable flag. No live interception test was performed.
findings.expected: Only the launcher and its worker should have access to the private request/reply channel and startup report.
findings.observed: The Unix launcher retains two ordinary pipes. On Linux their inodes can be reopened by a separate process with matching credentials when the launcher is dumpable and procfs and the LSM allow it. The worker's own restrictions leave the launcher ends unchanged. The receiving side validates report bytes and framing but assumes exclusive endpoints.
findings.impact: Local confidentiality and message integrity can be lost for data sent through the pipes, including the startup admission report and forwarded secret data. A peer can also invalidate the assumption of exclusive I/O during a timed exchange. This requires ordinary same-user access as permitted by host policy; privileged debugging and application code execution are unnecessary. Secrets held entirely within the worker do not cross these pipes.
findings.recommendedFix: Use a transport that preserves endpoint ownership over both launcher and child lifetimes. Document the parent-process trust boundary and make startup and timed I/O rely on enforceable transport properties.
findings.requiredVerification: Verify endpoint exclusivity from process creation through teardown under the supported Linux policies. Retest the ordinary synthetic worker protocol and timed I/O.

findings.title: Native allocation accepts sizes outside Rust slice limits
findings.evidence: Two independent static reviews, the Rust slice safety contract and the mmap contract. Existing oversized WorkArea test passes on x86-64 and cross-Clippy succeeds on ARMv5; neither establishes that the crate itself rejects the size before a native reservation on a 32-bit host.
findings.expected: The native mapping boundary guarantees that every Rust slice built from its mapping is at most isize::MAX bytes, and fallible API paths reject unsupported sizes before mapping.
findings.observed: Unix reservation bounds page rounding and guard-page arithmetic in usize but omits the isize::MAX contract. Allocation owners and stack wiping form raw slices from the stored native length. Linux mmap can accept an object larger than PTRDIFF_MAX, the corresponding C limit.
findings.impact: Unsound safe API if a 32-bit process can reserve enough contiguous virtual address space. Documented Linux 32-bit support is affected conditionally. The Windows native boundary likewise relies on OS refusal, although the tested 64-bit configuration has a much smaller usable address range than isize::MAX. No runtime undefined behavior was observed.
findings.recommendedFix: Enforce the slice-layout size bound in the common native allocation contract, including the protected stack's wipe length after rounding and each raw-slice call site.
findings.requiredVerification: Exercise the size validation independently of allocator success and run the bounded regression on 32-bit native Linux.

findings.title: Timed worker start traps on WebAssembly
findings.evidence: Static dispatch review and retained exact-commit V8 contract output from AUD-019, local wasm-contract-5cea35f.log.
findings.expected: Worker start methods report Unsupported on wasm32-unknown-unknown.
findings.observed: The timed variant calls Instant::now before reaching the unsupported-platform implementation, resulting in a WebAssembly trap. The ordinary start and terminal variant reach the unsupported path.
findings.impact: A portable caller using the timed entry point loses error handling in its WebAssembly runtime. The supported WebAssembly buffer operations are unaffected.
findings.recommendedFix: Dispatch unsupported platforms before reading the clock.
findings.requiredVerification: Check all start variants in a WebAssembly runtime, including zero-duration timeout input. Keep existing native timed-start behavior.

findings.title: Unix exchange can return a transport error after its deadline
findings.evidence: Source-order check of the common Unix startup report and application exchange path. No timing-sensitive runtime case was added.
findings.expected: A completed or failed exchange observed beyond the promised deadline produces TimedOut.
findings.observed: Unix returns the exchange error before the final clock check. A transport failure observed after the deadline can therefore retain its transport kind, while a late success becomes TimedOut.
findings.impact: Code distinguishing timeouts from broken transport can take the wrong error branch; failed calls still close the connection.
findings.recommendedFix: Define one clock/error precedence rule and apply it consistently to all final exchange results.
findings.requiredVerification: Use a deterministic completion seam to check that early errors retain their kind and late errors and successes use TimedOut.

findings.title: Unix terminal drain can exceed its documented byte budget
findings.evidence: Source-order and byte accounting of the Unix terminal drain. The separate late-arrival interval between drain and restoration remains a coverage gap.
findings.expected: Each Unix drain discards at most 64 KiB.
findings.observed: The drain issues a full 256-byte read before checking the cumulative total. A read past the budget can consume up to an extra 256 bytes before reporting failure.
findings.impact: More input can be discarded than the caller has been told, and an error follows after the extra read.
findings.recommendedFix: Apply the budget before reading; specify separately how the implementation detects pending input once the budget is exhausted.
findings.requiredVerification: Cover below-limit, exact-limit and over-limit input with bounded synthetic data and verify documented restore behavior.

findings.title: Windows thread identity documentation names an unused API
findings.evidence: Trace of thread handle selection, pinned liveness and process owner verification, with a production search for CompareObjectHandles.
findings.expected: The Windows security explanation identifies the production liveness and ownership checks.
findings.observed: The technical guide claims CompareObjectHandles. The code uses a retained handle and a liveness check, and validates process ownership where it opens by numeric thread ID.
findings.impact: Readers relying on the description can infer a stronger or different check than the one actually run.
findings.recommendedFix: Describe the actual handle lifetime and identity checks, including the two roster phases.
findings.requiredVerification: Compare the updated explanation to both retained-handle and ID-based paths.

findings.title: The development API guide mixes release versions
findings.evidence: Compared the guide with the public exports and source at v0.1.1 and at the reviewed commit.
findings.expected: A reader installing the documented version can use that guide's examples or is directed to the version-specific guide.
findings.observed: The installation and provenance example correctly describes published v0.1.1, but the same guide documents and uses methods introduced in 0.2.0 without distinguishing them at the entry point.
findings.impact: A reader following the installation snippet can try APIs absent from the installed crate. The old tag and its digest remain valid for their release.
findings.recommendedFix: Label the development guide and link the matching published version, then bind the final 0.2.0 commands to the eventual artifact and source tag.
findings.requiredVerification: Check the installation examples against their stated versions and verify the final package's attestation.

findings.title: Folder-write summaries omit conditions required by the implementation
findings.evidence: Cross-checked the README and API summary with the outcome model, platform caveats and SECURITY.md.
findings.expected: The summary makes the confirmed FolderWrites outcome and existing-channel exceptions visible at the point of use.
findings.observed: The overview states that entering with folders lets an application write there and nowhere else. A grant can be refused or have limited reach, and existing channels stay usable as explained further down the guide.
findings.impact: A caller can rely on omitted conditions when choosing its isolation check and write path.
findings.recommendedFix: Qualify the summary with the required outcome and scope and link the existing-channel and platform limitations where the operation is introduced.
findings.requiredVerification: Compare the supported, refused and pre-existing channel cases against the summary.

findings.title: The packaged notices link to an omitted workspace lockfile
findings.evidence: Inspected both byte-identical local crate archives and compared archive entries with the Git tree.
findings.expected: The published crate's notices resolve the separate development lockfile reference or identify it as repository-only.
findings.observed: The .crate contains THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md but omits fuzz/Cargo.lock along with the nested fuzz package. The notices link is relative.
findings.impact: Unpacked crate readers cannot follow that link. The root dependency notice comparison and root lockfile are intact.
findings.recommendedFix: Link to the repository location or label the development lockfile as present only in the checkout.
findings.requiredVerification: Check links from the next unpacked package as well as in the checkout.

informationalObservations: The preliminary coverage retained from AUD-019 for the same source was 3,744 of 3,961 lines. The current run hit 3,743 lines. Use the current measurement independently and retain both raw outputs. The README and coverage guide currently label the prior measurement; refresh their headline with the new release candidate after remediation.

The existing fix register explains the two relative AUD-001 links to an old test path and points to the original published source. Existing pending platform-specific dispositions are kept as recorded unless a finding-specific test demonstrated the case.
AUD-019 and AUD-020 were already occupied by independent local evidence. This report uses AUD-021 and references retained results with identity and scope.
limitations: The high Linux IPC finding and 32-bit layout finding are established by source and OS contracts; there was no runtime demonstration of IPC access or undefined behavior.
Android, iOS, 32-bit Linux and Windows GNU received cross-target Clippy rather than native runtime here. WASM had a focused retained V8 run. CI exercises Windows on its native runner.

Windows real-console input, macOS ACL and ignore-ownership volumes, the collided-name and repeated-grant macOS cases, and the optional Linux branches requiring unavailable host policy remain outside the demonstrated acceptance matrix.
Historical harness implementations, external dependencies in full, and published package signatures and attestations for the eventual release are outside the newly executed checks.

Adjacent AUD-019 ASan, Miri and optimized disassembly logs remain local supplementary evidence. This report does not credit them as completed acceptance checks because it did not rebind each tool input and result to the exact audited artifact.

The SGR/UTF-8 terminal suites do not establish behavior for bytes arriving in the interval between the final drain and restore. The documented effective intersection of Linux signal filters after fork was checked and is not an open defect.
